L233@P5: Special populations
L234@P5: Paediatric population
L235@P5: There is no experience in children with CML below 2 years of age and with Ph+ALL below 1 year of
L236@P5: age (see section 5.1). There is very limited experience in children with MDS/MPD, DFSP, GIST and
L237@P5-6: HES/CEL.7
L238@P6: The safety and efficacy of imatinib in children with MDS/MPD, DFSP, GIST and HES/CEL aged less
L239@P6: than 18 years of age have not been established in clinical trials. Currently available published data are
L240@P6: summarised in section 5.1 but no recommendation on a posology can be made.
L241@P6: Hepatic insufficiency
L242@P6: Imatinib is mainly metabolised through the liver. Patients with mild, moderate or severe liver
L243@P6: dysfunction should be given the minimum recommended dose of 400 mg daily. The dose can be
L244@P6: reduced if not tolerated (see sections 4.4, 4.8 and 5.2).
L245@P6: Liver dysfunction classification:
L246@P6: Liver dysfunction Liver function tests
L247@P6: Mild Total bilirubin: = 1.5 ULN
L248@P6: AST: > ULN (can be normal or < ULN if total bilirubin is
L249@P6: > ULN)

L251@P6: AST: any
L252@P6: Severe Total bilirubin: > 3–10 ULN
L253@P6: AST: any
L254@P6: ULN = upper limit of normal for the institution
L255@P6: AST = aspartate aminotransferase
L256@P6: Renal insufficiency
L257@P6: Patients with renal dysfunction or on dialysis should be given the minimum recommended dose of
L258@P6: 400 mg daily as starting dose. However, in these patients caution is recommended. The dose can be
L259@P6: reduced if not tolerated. If tolerated, the dose can be increased for lack of efficacy (see sections 4.4
L260@P6: and 5.2).
L261@P6: Older people
L262@P6: Imatinib pharmacokinetics have not been specifically studied in older people. No significant agerelated pharmacokinetic differences have been observed in adult patients in clinical trials which
L263@P6: included over 20% of patients age 65 and older. No specific dose recommendation is necessary in
L264@P6: older people.
L265@P6: 4.3 Contraindications
L266@P6: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
L267@P6: 4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use
L268@P6: When Glivec is co-administered with other medicinal products, there is a potential for drug
L269@P6: interactions. Caution should be used when taking Glivec with protease inhibitors, azole antifungals,
L270@P6: certain macrolides (see section 4.5), CYP3A4 substrates with a narrow therapeutic window (e.g.
L271@P6: cyclosporine, pimozide, tacrolimus, sirolimus, ergotamine, diergotamine, fentanyl, alfentanil,
L272@P6: terfenadine, bortezomib, docetaxel, quinidine) or warfarin and other coumarin derivatives (see
L273@P6: section 4.5).
L274@P6: Concomitant use of imatinib and medicinal products that induce CYP3A4 (e.g. dexamethasone,
L275@P6: phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin, phenobarbital or Hypericum perforatum, also known as St.
L276@P6: John’s Wort) may significantly reduce exposure to Glivec, potentially increasing the risk of
L277@P6: therapeutic failure. Therefore, concomitant use of strong CYP3A4 inducers and imatinib should be
L278@P6-7: avoided (see section 4.5).8
L279@P7: Hypothyroidism
L280@P7: Clinical cases of hypothyroidism have been reported in thyroidectomy patients undergoing
L281@P7: levothyroxine replacement during treatment with Glivec (see section 4.5). Thyroid-stimulating
L282@P7: hormone (TSH) levels should be closely monitored in such patients.
L283@P7: Hepatotoxicity
L284@P7: Metabolism of Glivec is mainly hepatic, and only 13% of excretion is through the kidneys. In patients
L285@P7: with hepatic dysfunction (mild, moderate or severe), peripheral blood counts and liver enzymes should
L286@P7: be carefully monitored (see sections 4.2, 4.8 and 5.2). It should be noted that GIST patients may have
L287@P7: hepatic metastases which could lead to hepatic impairment.
L288@P7: Cases of liver injury, including hepatic failure and hepatic necrosis, have been observed with imatinib.
L289@P7: When imatinib is combined with high dose chemotherapy regimens, an increase in serious hepatic
L290@P7: reactions has been detected. Hepatic function should be carefully monitored in circumstances where
L291@P7: imatinib is combined with chemotherapy regimens also known to be associated with hepatic
L292@P7: dysfunction (see sections 4.5 and 4.8).
L293@P7: Fluid retention
L294@P7: Occurrences of severe fluid retention (pleural effusion, oedema, pulmonary oedema, ascites,
L295@P7: superficial oedema) have been reported in approximately 2.5% of newly diagnosed CML patients
L296@P7: taking Glivec. Therefore, it is highly recommended that patients be weighed regularly. An unexpected
L297@P7: rapid weight gain should be carefully investigated and if necessary appropriate supportive care and
L298@P7: therapeutic measures should be undertaken. In clinical trials, there was an increased incidence of these
L299@P7: events in older people and those with a prior history of cardiac disease. Therefore, caution should be
L300@P7: exercised in patients with cardiac dysfunction.
L301@P7: Patients with cardiac disease
L302@P7: Patients with cardiac disease, risk factors for cardiac failure or history of renal failure should be
L303@P7: monitored carefully, and any patient with signs or symptoms consistent with cardiac or renal failure
L304@P7: should be evaluated and treated.
L305@P7: In patients with hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with occult infiltration of HES cells within the
L306@P7: myocardium, isolated cases of cardiogenic shock/left ventricular dysfunction have been associated
L307@P7: with HES cell degranulation upon the initiation of imatinib therapy. The condition was reported to be
L308@P7: reversible with the administration of systemic steroids, circulatory support measures and temporarily
L309@P7: withholding imatinib. As cardiac adverse events have been reported uncommonly with imatinib, a
L310@P7: careful assessment of the benefit/risk of imatinib therapy should be considered in the HES/CEL

L1387@P31: metabolites.
L1388@P31: The in vitro results showed that CYP3A4 was the major human P450 enzyme catalysing the
L1389@P31: biotransformation of imatinib. Of a panel of potential comedications (acetaminophen, aciclovir,
L1390@P31: allopurinol, amphotericin, cytarabine, erythromycin, fluconazole, hydroxyurea, norfloxacin, penicillin
L1391@P31: V) only erythromycin (IC50 50 µM) and fluconazole (IC50 118 µM) showed inhibition of imatinib
L1392@P31: metabolism which could have clinical relevance.
L1393@P31: Imatinib was shown in vitro to be a competitive inhibitor of marker substrates for CYP2C9, CYP2D6
L1394@P31: and CYP3A4/5. Ki values in human liver microsomes were 27, 7.5 and 7.9 mol/l, respectively.
L1395@P31: Maximal plasma concentrations of imatinib in patients are 2–4 mol/l, consequently an inhibition of
L1396@P31: CYP2D6 and/or CYP3A4/5-mediated metabolism of co-administered drugs is possible. Imatinib did
L1397@P31: not interfere with the biotransformation of 5-fluorouracil, but it inhibited paclitaxel metabolism as a
L1398@P31: result of competitive inhibition of CYP2C8 (Ki = 34.7 µM). This Ki value is far higher than the
L1399@P31: expected plasma levels of imatinib in patients, consequently no interaction is expected upon coadministration of either 5-fluorouracil or paclitaxel and imatinib.
L1400@P31: Elimination
L1401@P31: Based on the recovery of compound(s) after an oral 14C-labelled dose of imatinib, approximately 81%
L1402@P31: of the dose was recovered within 7 days in faeces (68% of dose) and urine (13% of dose). Unchanged
L1403@P31-32: imatinib accounted for 25% of the dose (5% urine, 20% faeces), the remainder being metabolites.33
L1404@P32: Plasma pharmacokinetics
L1405@P32: Following oral administration in healthy volunteers, the t½ was approximately 18 h, suggesting that
L1406@P32: once-daily dosing is appropriate. The increase in mean AUC with increasing dose was linear and dose
L1407@P32: proportional in the range of 25–1 000 mg imatinib after oral administration. There was no change in
L1408@P32: the kinetics of imatinib on repeated dosing, and accumulation was 1.5–2.5-fold at steady state when
L1409@P32: dosed once daily.
L1410@P32: Pharmacokinetics in GIST patients
L1411@P32: In patients with GIST steady-state exposure was 1.5-fold higher than that observed for CML patients
L1412@P32: for the same dosage (400 mg daily). Based on preliminary population pharmacokinetic analysis in
L1413@P32: GIST patients, there were three variables (albumin, WBC and bilirubin) found to have a statistically
L1414@P32: significant relationship with imatinib pharmacokinetics. Decreased values of albumin caused a
L1415@P32: reduced clearance (CL/f); and higher levels of WBC led to a reduction of CL/f. However, these
L1416@P32: associations are not sufficiently pronounced to warrant dose adjustment. In this patient population, the
L1417@P32: presence of hepatic metastases could potentially lead to hepatic insufficiency and reduced metabolism.
L1418@P32: Population pharmacokinetics
L1419@P32: Based on population pharmacokinetic analysis in CML patients, there was a small effect of age on the
L1420@P32: volume of distribution (12% increase in patients > 65 years old). This change is not thought to be
L1421@P32: clinically significant. The effect of bodyweight on the clearance of imatinib is such that for a patient
L1422@P32: weighing 50 kg the mean clearance is expected to be 8.5 l/h, while for a patient weighing 100 kg the
L1423@P32: clearance will rise to 11.8 l/h. These changes are not considered sufficient to warrant dose adjustment
L1424@P32: based on kg bodyweight. There is no effect of gender on the kinetics of imatinib.
L1425@P32: Pharmacokinetics in children
L1426@P32: As in adult patients, imatinib was rapidly absorbed after oral administration in paediatric patients in
L1427@P32: both phase I and phase II studies. Dosing in children at 260 and 340 mg/m2/day achieved the same
L1428@P32: exposure, respectively, as doses of 400 mg and 600 mg in adult patients. The comparison of AUC(0-24)
L1429@P32: on day 8 and day 1 at the 340 mg/m2/day dose level revealed a 1.7-fold drug accumulation after
L1430@P32: repeated once-daily dosing.
L1431@P32: Based on pooled population pharmacokinetic analysis in paediatric patients with haematological
L1432@P32: disorders (CML, Ph+ALL, or other haematological disorders treated with imatinib), clearance of
L1433@P32: imatinib increases with increasing body surface area (BSA). After correcting for the BSA effect, other
L1434@P32: demographics such as age, body weight and body mass index did not have clinically significant effects
L1435@P32: on the exposure of imatinib. The analysis confirmed that exposure of imatinib in paediatric patients
L1436@P32: receiving 260 mg/m2once daily (not exceeding 400 mg once daily) or 340 mg/m2once daily (not
L1437@P32: exceeding 600 mg once daily) were similar to those in adult patients who received imatinib 400 mg or
L1438@P32: 600 mg once daily.
L1439@P32: Organ function impairment
L1440@P32: Imatinib and its metabolites are not excreted via the kidney to a significant extent. Patients with mild
L1441@P32: and moderate impairment of renal function appear to have a higher plasma exposure than patients with
L1442@P32: normal renal function. The increase is approximately 1.5- to 2-fold, corresponding to a 1.5-fold
L1443@P32: elevation of plasma AGP, to which imatinib binds strongly. The free drug clearance of imatinib is
L1444@P32: probably similar between patients with renal impairment and those with normal renal function, since
L1445@P32: renal excretion represents only a minor elimination pathway for imatinib (see sections 4.2 and 4.4).
L1446@P32: Although the results of pharmacokinetic analysis showed that there is considerable inter-subject
L1447@P32: variation, the mean exposure to imatinib did not increase in patients with varying degrees of liver
L1448@P32-33: dysfunction as compared to patients with normal liver function (see sections 4.2, 4.4 and 4.8).34
L1449@P33: 5.3 Preclinical safety data
L1450@P33: The preclinical safety profile of imatinib was assessed in rats, dogs, monkeys and rabbits.
L1451@P33: Multiple dose toxicity studies revealed mild to moderate haematological changes in rats, dogs and
L1452@P33: monkeys, accompanied by bone marrow changes in rats and dogs.
L1453@P33: The liver was a target organ in rats and dogs. Mild to moderate increases in transaminases and slight
L1454@P33: decreases in cholesterol, triglycerides, total protein and albumin levels were observed in both species.
L1455@P33: No histopathological changes were seen in rat liver. Severe liver toxicity was observed in dogs treated
L1456@P33: for 2 weeks, with elevated liver enzymes, hepatocellular necrosis, bile duct necrosis, and bile duct
L1457@P33: hyperplasia.
L1458@P33: Renal toxicity was observed in monkeys treated for 2 weeks, with focal mineralisation and dilation of
L1459@P33: the renal tubules and tubular nephrosis. Increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine were
L1460@P33: observed in several of these animals. In rats, hyperplasia of the transitional epithelium in the renal
L1461@P33: papilla and in the urinary bladder was observed at doses  6 mg/kg in the 13-week study, without
L1462@P33: changes in serum or urinary parameters. An increased rate of opportunistic infections was observed
L1463@P33: with chronic imatinib treatment.
L1464@P33: In a 39-week monkey study, no NOAEL (no observed adverse effect level) was established at the
L1465@P33: lowest dose of 15 mg/kg, approximately one-third the maximum human dose of 800 mg based on
L1466@P33: body surface. Treatment resulted in worsening of normally suppressed malarial infections in these
L1467@P33: animals.
L1468@P33: Imatinib was not considered genotoxic when tested in an in vitro bacterial cell assay (Ames test), an in
L1469@P33: vitro mammalian cell assay (mouse lymphoma) and an in vivo rat micronucleus test. Positive
